name: state-colocation
intent: Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it.
problem: State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.
context: Declarative component UIs (React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Compose, Blazor, Qt Quick) and, in generalized form, any system where a mutable value is owned by one component-like unit: the consumers determine the state's scope, the framework invalidates only what the owner's subtree can observe, and components are composed, moved and deleted. Most compelling where over-lifted or global state has already become a performance and ownership problem.
benefits: Locality of behaviour: the state sits beside the code that reads and writes it, so they change, move and get deleted together (place code as close to where it is relevant as possible).
Update cost is bounded by the consumers: a change invalidates only the owner's subtree instead of the whole component tree, which is the documented performance rationale for moving state down.
Ownership becomes explicit: one component declares each value, so there is no question who may write it and no second copy to keep in sync.
Props stop carrying values nobody reads: purely local state needs no prop types, no threading through intermediate layers and no context plumbing.
Components become self-contained: one that owns its state can be tested, reused, moved between screens or published on its own.

It replaces a default with a decision procedure: start local, lift to the closest common parent only when a second consumer appears, and mount providers as low as their consumers allow — which also keeps the global store small.
tradeoffs: Re-lifting is a real refactor: as soon as a second consumer appears, the owner must change — state moves up, an updater callback is threaded down, props/types/context change. The pattern defers that cost, it does not remove it.

Eager colocation creates duplicates: two components that need the same logical value each keep their own copy and the copies drift, which is worse than the over-lifted state the pattern set out to avoid.
Splitting a component for state adds layers: giving a cell a natural home often means introducing a wrapper component that exists only to hold it, adding depth and indirection to the tree.

Local state dies with its owner: remounting, navigation, changed keys and conditional rendering discard colocated state unless the framework's persistence mechanism (rememberSaveable, state restoration, URL parameters) is used deliberately.

The payoff depends on the framework: only rendering or observation models that scope invalidation to the readers gain the performance benefit; where updates are broad, colocation is mostly a maintenance decision.

Cross-cutting needs have to be lifted back out: URL synchronization, telemetry, undo/redo and persistence must reach the owning component or be pulled up, which is deliberate work the pattern does not do for you.
Nothing enforces it: the rule is a discipline, so over-lifting is caught in review or measured, not rejected by a compiler or linter.

participants.responsibility: The component (or, in the generalized form, the module/object) that declares the state cell and is the only place where it is created, initialised and primarily written.
The components that read the state, directly or through props/bindings; their extent defines how far a change may propagate and therefore how much of the view an update touches.
The lowest ancestor that contains every consumer; the promotion target when a second consumer appears, so the value is lifted exactly as far as it must be and no further.
Context, provider or state holder used when consumers are too far apart for props; mounted as low in the tree as the shared consumers allow rather than at the root.
The application-level owner reserved for genuinely global, long-lived state (session/identity, server cache, cross-route data); explicitly the exception, not the default home for UI state.

use_cases: A search or form input whose value is read only by the input, its own validation and its own preview: keep it in that component instead of the screen root (the canonical typing example where hoisting made every keystroke re-render the page).
Which panel of an accordion is open: leave it per panel while panels are independent, then lift exactly to the accordion once only one panel may be open at a time (the closest common parent).
Tooltip, hover, popover and dropdown state in a chart or table cell: own it in the cell component rather than in a global UI store.
Per-row edit or selection state in a data grid: the row component owns it; only cross-row operations need the grid to own it.
Dialog and modal open state in the button or list that opens it, until another surface must close or observe it.
Form draft state in the form component; lift it only when a sibling — summary panel, preview pane, wizard footer — genuinely must read it.
Extracting a self-contained widget for reuse or publication: keeping its state local makes the component portable and shrinks its API.
Per-cell expansion state in a tree view or file explorer: the tree node component owns whether it is expanded; the parent tree only coordinates multi-select or bulk-expand operations.

Media playback state for a single player (play/pause, current time, volume): colocate in the player component rather than a global audio store unless the same track plays in multiple places simultaneously.
Local filter/sort state for a data table or list: keep it in the list component until a URL parameter, shareable link, or sibling panel requires sharing it.
Vue: composable-local state (useSearch, useToggle) where each consumer needs its own independent instance of the same reactive logic pattern.
Angular Signals: feature-level signal stores scoped to a route or feature slice, not the entire application store, for UI state and feature-derived state.

SwiftUI: @State for view-local value types; @StateObject for view-owned reference types; keep @EnvironmentObject for genuinely cross-cutting state (auth session, theme) mounted as low in the hierarchy as consumers allow.

Svelte 5 runes: `let count = $state(0)` inside a component is per-component-instance reactive state — the component that declares it is its owner; Svelte's v5 migration explicitly replaced the pre-runes habit of reaching for a store whenever state sat at a component's top level, with $state plus $derived/$effect as the local cells, and module-level .svelte.js state only for deliberate sharing.

Jetpack Compose: the official hoisting guidance is this pattern's placement ladder — keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist only to the lowest common ancestor of all composables that read or write it, pass value down and onValueChange up, and make the ViewModel the owner only when business logic or lifecycle outlives the composition.

Blazor: component fields are the default owner for UI-local state; the official state-management guidance promotes to an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state, and to Protected Browser Storage only when the value must survive circuits or sessions — a three-rung ladder that mirrors local state, scoped provider, persistence.
avoid_when: Several distant components share one value: lift it to the closest common parent, or use a scoped provider mounted as low as the consumers allow, instead of duplicating the value locally.

The value must survive unmounting, navigation or reload: use the framework's persistence mechanism (URL/query parameters, session or persistent storage, rememberSaveable, PersistentComponentState) rather than colocated component state.
The value is server data rather than UI state: a query cache or store owns it; copying it into component state creates a second source of truth.
The value must be observable outside the view tree (devtools, analytics, undo, cross-tab synchronization): a store or a reducer-style model is the appropriate owner.
The value is genuinely application-scoped (session, theme, locale, feature flags): give it one deliberate app-level owner instead of forcing artificial colocation.
High-frequency updates (mouse position, animation frames, real-time data): use a signals library or direct DOM manipulation; context and even many global stores will re-render too many consumers.
The value is computed from other state: derive it in place rather than storing it twice and risking the copies drifting.
anti_patterns: Root-by-default state: every value lifted to the application root or one global store 'just in case', so any change invalidates the tree and no value has a traceable owner.
Fake colocation: the same logical value declared in two sibling components that then drift, instead of lifting it to their closest common parent.
Wrapper-only components: splitting a component solely to give state a home, adding tree depth and indirection without behaviour.
Store as a generic bucket: transient UI state (hover, draft text, open/closed) pushed into Redux/MVI/Bloc, producing store churn, noisy devtools and re-render amplification.
Reading across the tree: reaching into a child's colocated state through refs, parent pointers or selectors instead of lifting it deliberately, turning a private cell into hidden public state.
Premature URL promotion: putting every piece of transient UI state into URL parameters because 'it might be bookmarked' — pollutes the URL and complicates routing.
design_principles: Locality of behaviour: place state as close to the code that uses it as possible; things that change together belong together.
Single source of truth: exactly one owner per piece of state; everything else is derived or passed down.
Information hiding: a component's internal state is an implementation detail, not part of its interface.
Least scope (YAGNI applied to state): choose the narrowest scope that satisfies the current consumers and widen only for a real second consumer.
Separation of concerns with a bounded blast radius: keep each change local to the unit that can observe it.
State lifetime is explicit: state that must survive navigation or remounting belongs in a persistence mechanism, not in a component.
best_practices: Start local: declare the state in the component that first reads it, and treat every lift as a deliberate promotion rather than the default.
When a second consumer appears, lift exactly to the closest common parent — value down, updater callback up — and not to the application root.
When consumers are far apart, use a scoped provider or state container mounted as low in the tree as the consumers allow; do not put every provider at the root.
Keep global stores for genuinely global, long-lived state (session/identity, server cache, cross-route data) and keep transient UI state out of them.
Derive what can be derived: only values that cannot be computed from existing state deserve their own cell.
Decide lifetime explicitly: if the value must survive remounting or navigation, put it in the framework's persistence mechanism instead of colocated state.
Split a component when its state has no natural home — a growing component usually hides several smaller owners — not merely to relocate a cell.
Re-run the decision procedure continuously: as the component tree evolves, previously colocated state may need to be lifted or moved to a provider.
In Vue, prefer local `ref` for component-only state; promote to a Pinia store only when two or more unrelated components need it, or when it must survive page navigation.
In Angular, use `signal()` for feature-scoped state at the component or route level; reserve app-level state (auth, theme) for `Environment` injection mounted as low as consumers require.

In SwiftUI, use `@State` for view-local value types, `@StateObject` for view-owned reference types, and `@EnvironmentObject` only for genuinely cross-cutting state; colocate ephemeral UI state (panel visibility, toggle) in the view that owns it.
Treat URL parameters as a first-class scoping layer: when state must be shareable, bookmarkable, or survive refresh, the URL is a better home than a store — not a fallback for colocated state.
Separate server state from UI state: server data (API responses, cached queries) belongs in a server-state library (TanStack Query, SWR), not in component state or a global store.

Group context by domain, not by app: split `ThemeContext`, `AuthContext`, `CartContext` rather than one monolithic `AppContext` — each domain-specific context triggers re-renders only in its own consumers.
Memoize context values with `useMemo`/`useCallback` to avoid publishing new object identities on every render, which forces re-renders in all consumers regardless of whether data changed.
sources: Dodds, K. C., 'State Colocation will make your React app faster' (2019) — names state colocation for component state, gives the decision procedure (used only by this component: leave it; used by one child: colocate; used by a sibling or parent: lift) and the performance rationale (reducing the re-render scope from the full tree to only the consumer subtree). https://kentcdodds.com/blog/state-colocation-will-make-your-react-app-faster

Dodds, K. C., 'Colocation' (2019) — the underlying principle: 'place code as close to where it's relevant as possible', with state as one of its key applications. https://kentcdodds.com/blog/colocation

Dodds, K. C., 'Application State Management with React' (2019) — makes the case that React itself is the state management library, and that state should be colocated in the component tree; also covers when to reach for context and when for an external store. https://kentcdodds.com/blog/application-state-management-with-react

Dodds, K. C., 'One simple trick to optimize React re-renders' (2019) — demonstrates that moving a slow component to be rendered by a parent that re-renders less often is a free performance win via identity-based bailout, closely related to colocation. https://kentcdodds.com/blog/optimize-react-re-renders

React documentation, 'Sharing State Between Components' — lifting state to the closest common parent, and the controlled/uncontrolled distinction behind colocated state. https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components
React documentation, 'Managing State' — structuring state well, avoiding redundant/duplicate state, and the single source of truth principle. https://react.dev/learn/managing-state
React documentation, 'useState' reference — the component-local state cell as a hook called at the top level of the component that owns the value. https://react.dev/reference/react/useState

Abramov, D., 'Presentational and Container Components' (2015) — the foundational pattern for separating stateful logic (container) from pure rendering (presentational); Dan Abramov later walked back parts of this in 2019 as hooks made the distinction less necessary. https://medium.com/@dan_abramov/smart-and-dumb-components-7ca2f9a7c7d0

Redux documentation, 'Usage with React — Presentational and Container Components' — official guidance on separating presentational and container components with React Redux's `connect()`. https://redux.js.org/docs/basics/UsageWithReact.html

Vue.js documentation, 'State Management' — extracting shared reactive state into module-level singletons via `reactive()`, and Pinia as the recommended store; also covers local `ref` as the first resort. https://vuejs.org/guide/scaling-up/state-management.html

Pinia documentation, 'Introduction' and 'Core Concepts' — Pinia as Vue's official store, setup vs option stores, `$subscribe` for state observation, and `storeToRefs` for reactive destructuring. https://pinia.vuejs.org

Vue Wiki, 'When should you use Pinia vs a composable vs local state?' — decision tree: local `ref` for one component, composable for reusable per-consumer instances, Pinia for multi-component shared state that must survive navigation; warns against Pinia overuse for single-component state. https://vuewiki.dev/q/pinia-vs-composable-vs-local

VueUse documentation / Antfu, 'State Management Strategy' — keep state local first, promote to shared/global only when needed; singleton composables only for non-SSR apps; prefer Pinia for SSR/Nuxt, large apps, and cases requiring DevTools or action tracing. https://github.com/antfu/skills/blob/main/skills/vue-best-practices/references/state-management.md

Angular documentation, 'Signals Overview' — Angular's signal as a reactive value container that notifies consumers on change, with `signal()`, `computed()`, `effect()`, and `WritableSignal.asReadonly()` for explicit ownership. https://angular.dev/guide/signals

Angular Team / modernfrontendarchitecture.com, 'Angular Signals State Management Enterprise Guide 2026' — signals as a feature-level state primitive; hybrid model of signals for synchronous feature state, RxJS for async orchestration, and global NgRx/Redux only for genuinely cross-cutting concerns; route-scoped provider defaults. https://modernfrontendarchitecture.com/articles/angular-signals-enterprise-state/

Apple documentation, 'Managing model data in your app' — SwiftUI `@State` for view-owned value types, `@StateObject` for view-owned reference types, `@Environment`/`@EnvironmentObject` for cross-cutting state injected as low in the hierarchy as consumers require; `@ObservedObject` for state received from a parent. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/managing-model-data-in-your-app

Apple documentation, 'StateObject' — the ownership distinction between `@StateObject` (owner, instantiated once per view container) and `@ObservedObject` (observer, receives from parent); lifecycle tied to view identity. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/stateobject/

Hudson, P., 'What is the difference between @ObservedObject, @State, and @EnvironmentObject?' (2021) — practical decision guide: `@State` for simple view-local value types, `@ObservedObject` for external reference types, `@StateObject` once per owner, `@EnvironmentObject` for truly shared app-wide state. https://www.hackingwithswift.com/quick-start/swiftui/whats-the-difference-between-observedobject-state-and-environmentobject

van der Lee, A., '@StateObject vs @ObservedObject: The differences explained' (2026) — concrete rule: does this view create the object? Use `@StateObject`. Does the view receive it from a parent? Use `@ObservedObject`. Failure to distinguish causes state loss on view recreation. https://www.avanderlee.com/swiftui/stateobject-observedobject-differences/

React team / OpenReplay, 'Reactivity Models Compared: React, Vue, Angular, Svelte' (2026) — signals convergence across frameworks; React's coarse-grained model vs Vue/Angular/Svelte fine-grained dependency tracking; React 19 Compiler closes the gap via automatic memoization. https://blog.openreplay.com/reactivity-react-vue-angular-svelte/

OpenReplay / Sabaoon, 'Signals-Based Reactivity: Why Every Major Framework Is Abandoning the Virtual DOM' (2026) — TC39 signals proposal, Angular Signals replacing Zone.js, Svelte 5 runes as compiler-transformed signals, Vue `ref`/`reactive` as signals under a different name; performance implications for state scope decisions. https://www.sabaoon.dev/blog/signals-reactivity-frameworks-2026

Sabaoon, 'Why does a single state change in legacy Angular result in more work?' — Zone.js monkey-patches async APIs to trigger full top-down dirty-check vs Vue Proxy-based fine-grained tracking vs Svelte 5 compiled runes for targeted DOM bindings; Angular Signals pivot as the mitigation. https://tezvyn.com/bite/how-does-angulars-zone-js-change-detection-differ-from-vue-and-svelte-reactivity-b132da0e

NDLab blog, 'Understanding State Boundaries: Local, Shared, and Global' (2026) — decision matrix: one component → local state; few related components → lifted state; many distant components → context or store; URL/shareable → URL; server data → server state library. https://ndlab.blog/posts/part6-1-state-boundaries-react

Code Chronicles / Alalla, 'State Placement: Where Should This State Live?' (2026) — comprehensive decision tree for React state placement; warns against premature globalization, context for high-frequency updates, and duplicate server state in client state. https://blog.sandeepallala.com/blog/state-placement-where-should-state-live

FreeCodeCamp, 'Shared State Complexity in React — A Complete Handbook' (2025) — prop drilling pitfalls, context re-render costs, premature globalization, server state vs client state distinction; `useReducer` for complex co-located logic. https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/shared-state-complexity-in-react-handbook/

Stanza.dev, 'React Context API — Patterns, Pitfalls & React 19' (2026) — context as a broadcast mechanism, not a state manager; split contexts by domain; memoize context values; avoid for high-frequency updates; custom hooks for null-safety. https://www.stanza.dev/concepts/react-context-api

llmbestpractices.com, 'React State Management' (2026) — three-tier state: local `useState`, URL state, focused client store; rule of three for lifting; `useSyncExternalStore` for store subscriptions; server state not being client state. https://llmbestpractices.com/frontend/react-state-management

Dayvi Schuster, 'Three different states — Remote, App, and Local' (2024) — the three-state model: Remote (server/API), App (global cross-cutting), Local (component); sync App-to-Local only when needed; local-first reduces sync overhead and improves performance. https://dayvster.com/blog/the-three-states/

Epic React / Dodds, K. C., 'Improve the Performance of your React Forms' — form field state colocated per field vs hoisted to form; `FastInput` with local `useState` vs `SlowInput` receiving all form state as props; performance profiling showing 0ms total blocking time for colocated vs 112ms for hoisted. https://www.epicreact.dev/improve-the-performance-of-your-react-forms

Epic React / Dodds, K. C., 'Colocate State Workshop' (2024) — colocating state to where it is consumed; pushing state down to the component that needs it rather than keeping it at a parent. https://www.epicreact.dev/workshops/react-hooks/colocate-state/exercise

React Performance / Kent C. Dodds, 'Fix perf death by a thousand cuts' — colocating state solves perf problems caused by many components re-rendering unnecessarily on each state change; scoped providers as the solution for shared state while keeping the blast radius small. https://react-performance.netlify.app/6

Svelte documentation, '$state' — the rune declares reactive state owned by the component instance that declares it (deeply reactive proxy; `$state.raw`/`$state.snapshot` variants); module-level `.svelte.js` state is the deliberate sharing mechanism, keeping the component as the default owner. https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/$state

Svelte documentation, 'What are runes?' and 'Svelte 5 migration guide' — runes replace the pre-5 constraint that reactive state at a component's top level had to be lifted into a store for reuse, making per-component `$state` plus `$derived`/`$effect` the local cell and stores the explicit opt-in for sharing. https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/what-are-runes

Android Developers documentation, 'Where to hoist state | Jetpack Compose' — official placement ladder: keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, hoist to the lowest common ancestor of every composable that reads or writes it, avoid hoisting UI-only state into scopes that don't need it, and use the ViewModel only as the lifecycle-aware ancestor when business logic requires it. https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/state-hoisting

Microsoft Learn, 'ASP.NET Core Blazor state management' — component-owned fields by default; an in-memory state container service only when components must share non-persistent state; Protected Browser Storage / PersistentComponentState only when values must survive circuits, prerendering or sessions — the promotion ladder documented as official guidance. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/blazor/state-management?view=aspnetcore-9.0

Seram, N., 'Why your useState is in the wrong place' (2026) — criticism of the opposite failure mode to over-lifting: state colocated in the wrong component or made reactive 'just in case', causing unnecessary re-renders in every descendant of the shared owner; argues for counting actual consumers before choosing the cell. https://niteshseram.in/writing/usestate-in-the-wrong-place

Sethi, D., 'Most React state doesn't belong in React' (2026) — misuse critique of colocation-by-reflex: defaulting every mutable value to `useState` desynchronises it from browser-native owners (history/back button, URL, media elements) and produces mismatched UI; values the browser already tracks should be read, not re-owned. https://www.sethi.io/blog/most-react-state-doesnt-belong-in-react
